books.section: Christian Fundamentalism and the Religious Right

primary_sources: Roe v. Wade, January 22, 1973; Griswold v. Connecticut, 1965 (paraphrased)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Roe v. Wade (1973)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Roe v. Wade, January 22, 1973, and Griswold v. Connecticut, 1965. Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.14; 5 Steps Ch. 28; Princeton Ch. 12).
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Supreme Court's decision in Roe v. Wade, January 22, 1973. The Court held that the right to privacy, first recognized in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), covers a woman's decision to end a pregnancy, so states could not ban abortion in the early months of pregnancy. The decision struck down abortion bans in many states at once.

stem: Roe best explains which of the following developments in the 1970s?

options.text: It ended all religious involvement in American politics for good.
options.misconception: Background: After Roe, religious conservatives entered politics in greater numbers, the opposite of ending their involvement.

options.text: It made abortion a settled issue that no one debated afterward at all.
options.misconception: Background: Abortion stayed one of the most debated issues in American politics for decades after Roe.

options.text: It convinced evangelicals to stay out of elections and politics.
options.misconception: Background: After Roe, evangelicals organized to vote, through groups such as the Moral Majority.

options.text: It gave religious conservatives one issue that united evangelicals and Catholics in politics.

rationales.A: Background: After Roe, religious conservatives entered politics in greater numbers, the opposite of ending their involvement.
rationales.B: Background: Abortion stayed one of the most debated issues in American politics for decades after Roe.
rationales.C: Background: After Roe, evangelicals organized to vote, through groups such as the Moral Majority.
rationales.D: Roe struck down abortion bans in many states at once. Background: Opposition to abortion joined evangelicals and Catholics who had long kept apart.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says Roe struck down abortion bans in many states at once, in a single decision.
2. Background: Evangelicals and Catholics had long kept apart, but both opposed abortion.
3. One decision on one issue gave them a shared cause, and that shared cause built the Religious Right.
Remember: A single court decision can unite groups that agree on that one issue.
